cards.title: New York
cards.sub: 12 cards · ~27 min · to order in one sentence and be understood

cards.title: The bread that's boiled before it's baked
cards.body: Polish Jews brought it in the late nineteenth century, and the secret isn't the water, whatever people say: it's that the dough is boiled for a minute before going into the oven. That's what gives the shiny crust and the dense inside. The classic is with «lox», cured salmon — «laks» in Yiddish — cream cheese and onion. A good bagel has weight in the hand; if it's light and fluffy, it's a bread roll with a hole.

cards.title: You order in a single sentence
cards.body: The line moves fast and the person behind the counter has no patience: when it's your turn, say it all in one go. «Everything bagel, cream cheese, toasted». For the definitive New York breakfast, «bacon, egg and cheese on a roll», which here is ordered as «a BEC». Work it out before you reach the counter, not in front of it.

cards.question: You ask for «a slice» at a pizzeria. What do you get?
options: A thin triangle of pizza to eat standing up
cards.explain: A big triangle of thin pizza, folded in half and eaten walking or standing at the counter. It's the city's fast food, and for decades it cost the same as a subway ride: when one went up, so did the other. They call it «the pizza principle».

cards.title: The ticket you can't lose
cards.body: Pastrami is brined beef, smoked and then steamed, a recipe Romanian Jews brought over. Katz's, on the Lower East Side, has served it since 1888: you walk in, they hand you a ticket, the cutter makes it in front of you and writes the price on the ticket. You pay on the way out. Lose it and you pay a fine of tens of dollars, and they mean it.

cards.claim: «New York cheesecake really is from New York»
cards.body: The style, yes. Cheesecake goes back to ancient Greece, but the New York one is made with cream cheese, and that cheese was invented by a dairyman in New York State in 1872 while trying to copy a French one. Broadway restaurants made it famous in the thirties: dense, tall, no fruit on top. Everything else is a variation.

cards.question: How many restaurants are there in New York City?
cards.explain_correct: About 25,000, from every cuisine on the planet. You could eat dinner in a different one every night for nearly seventy years without repeating. And every week dozens close and open.
cards.explain_wrong: About 25,000, from every cuisine on the planet. You could eat dinner in a different one every night for nearly seventy years without repeating. And every week dozens close and open.

cards.title: Chicken over rice with white sauce
cards.body: On almost every Midtown corner there's a cart with a griddle serving «chicken over rice»: spiced chicken on yellow rice, salad, and a white sauce plus a red one that's genuinely hot. They started in the nineties feeding Muslim cab drivers who couldn't find halal food, and today they have a queue at lunchtime. For under ten dollars it's the best meal in the area.

cards.title: What the menu says isn't what you pay
cards.body: Prices are shown before tax: nearly 9% gets added to the bill, and the tip on top of that. A twenty-dollar dish ends up at twenty-six. Dinner is early, between six and eight, and on weekdays many kitchens close at ten. Weekend brunch is an institution with a queue: with no booking, you give your name and wait outside.

cards.question: You order «a regular coffee» at a deli. What do you get?
cards.explain: With milk and sugar, and plenty of both. In New York «regular» doesn't mean plain, it means that, and it's a classic trap for the newcomer. If you want it black, say «black». And it comes in the blue-and-white deli cup, an icon of the city.

cards.claim: «Pizza and bagels taste like this because of New York tap water»
cards.body: It's what every pizza maker in town says, and the water is good, from the Catskills reservoirs. But in blind tastings nobody can tell a dough made with New York water from any other; what matters is technique, a decades-old oven and volume: a place that makes a thousand pizzas a day makes them well. The water is the legend; the craft is the explanation.

cards.title: No egg, no cream
cards.body: The «egg cream» is the most New York drink there is and contains neither thing in its name: milk, seltzer and chocolate syrup, whipped until it foams. It was born in Brooklyn in the early twentieth century, at the soda fountains of the Jewish neighbourhoods, and a few old delis still serve it. Drink it straight away: in a minute the foam is dead.

cards.question: Someone suggests lunch at «a diner». What awaits you?
options: A restaurant with a huge menu, open nearly all hours
cards.explain: A neighbourhood restaurant with a twelve-page menu, vinyl booths, coffee refilled without asking and near round-the-clock hours. Breakfast, lunch and dinner all at once. It's where the TV shows eat, and where the city really eats.
